questions.prompt: Java Strings are immutable: `name.trim()` returns a new String and leaves `name` unchanged.
questions.explanation: String methods never modify the original object. You must use the returned value, e.g. name = name.trim().
`new String` creates a distinct object, so == (reference comparison) is false; equals compares the characters and is true. This is why tests compare text with equals or assertEquals.

questions.prompt: This price check fails on '£1,299.00'. What is the bug?
options: The comma remains in the string, so parseDouble throws NumberFormatException; remove thousands separators too (and consider BigDecimal for money)
replace must be replaceAll with a regex
The pound sign is not a char
questions.explanation: replace("£", "") leaves "1,299.00", and Double.parseDouble rejects the comma. Strip the separator as well. For money, BigDecimal avoids floating-point rounding issues.
i starts at 0 and the loop runs while i < 3, printing 0, 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: Why compare strings with `"expected".equals(actual)` rather than `actual.equals("expected")` in some helpers?
options: It avoids a NullPointerException if actual is null, returning false instead
questions.explanation: Calling equals on the literal is null-safe. Objects.equals(a, b) is another null-safe option. Neither form ignores case; that needs equalsIgnoreCase.

questions.prompt: A test reads a counter '12 items' from the page and must assert it increased by one after adding to cart. Which approach is most robust?
options: Extract the digits, parse them with Integer.parseInt, and assert after == before + 1
Convert both to double and compare with ==
questions.explanation: Parsing to an int and comparing numbers expresses the real rule. String contains '13' would pass for '113 items'; == on strings compares references; double equality is unnecessary for counts.
0.1 + 0.2 in binary floating point is 0.30000000000000004, so == 0.3 is false. Compare doubles with a tolerance (assertEquals(expected, actual, delta)) or use BigDecimal for money.

coding.title: Normalise text read from a page
coding.prompt:
Write a class `TextUtils` with a static method `String normalise(String s)` that:

- returns `""` for null,
- trims the ends,
- collapses any run of whitespace inside the text to a single space.

Example: `normalise("  Order   placed \n")` returns `"Order placed"`.
coding.explanation: Text read from a browser often has non-obvious whitespace (newlines, double spaces). Normalising in one helper keeps assertions simple. The null check comes first so the method never throws, and the regex \s+ matches any run of whitespace characters.
hints: Handle null before calling any method on s.
trim() removes leading and trailing whitespace.
coding.runInstructions: Create a Maven project with JUnit 5 (`org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter`, scope `test`). Put `TextUtils.java` in `src/main/java/` and `TextUtilsTest.java` in `src/test/java/`. Run `mvn test`; all tests should pass.

coding.title: Parse a displayed price
coding.prompt: Write a class `PriceParser` with a static method `java.math.BigDecimal parse(String text)` that turns displayed prices like `"£1,299.00"`, `"$ 5.5"` or `"12"` into a BigDecimal with **two decimal places** (`1299.00`, `5.50`, `12.00`). Remove any currency symbol, spaces and thousands separators (commas). Throw `IllegalArgumentException` if no digits remain.
coding.explanation: Keeping only digits and the decimal point strips symbols, spaces and separators in one step. BigDecimal represents money exactly, unlike double, and setScale(2) normalises the scale so that assertEquals(new BigDecimal("5.50"), ...) matches. Note BigDecimal.equals is scale-sensitive, which is why the scale must be fixed.
hints: A regex like [^0-9.] removes everything except digits and dots.
Check that at least one digit is left before building the BigDecimal.
coding.runInstructions: Create a Maven project with JUnit 5 (`org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter`, scope `test`). Put `PriceParser.java` in `src/main/java/` and `PriceParserTest.java` in `src/test/java/`. Run `mvn test`; all tests should pass.
